1	# Postgkyl
2	
3	![pytest](https://github.com/ammarhakim/postgkyl/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)
4	
5	This is the Postgkyl project. It is both Python library and command-line tool
6	designed to provide unified access to Gkeyll data together with a broad variety
7	of analytical and visualization tools.
8	
9	## Documentation
10	
11	Full documentation of the Gkeyll project is available at
12	[ReadTheDocs](http://gkeyll.rtfd.io).
13	
14	## Dependencies and Installation
15	
16	Postgkyl requires the packages listed in pyproject.toml
17	
18	Postgkyl requires NumPy >= 2.2.6. In addition, there is one optional
19	dependency:
20	
21	* [pytest](https://pypi.org/project/pytest/)
22	
23	[pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/) is required only for developers.
24	
25	### Setting up virtual environment (recommended)
26	
27	We strongly recommend creating a virtual Python environment for everybody
28	working with more than one Python project (this includes even using both
29	Postgkyl and Sphinx). The two recommended options are
30	[venv](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html) and
31	[mamba](https://mamba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).
32	
33	With `venv`, one can create the virtual environment with:
34	
35	```bash
36	python -m venv /path/to/new/virtual/environments/pgkyl
37	```
38	
39	then activate it with:
40	
41	| bash/zsh | `source <venv>/bin/activate`      |
42	| fish     | `source <venv>/bin/activate.fish` |
43	| csh/tcsh | `source <venv>/bin/activate.csh`  |
44	
45	and deactivate with:
46	
47	```bash
48	deactivate
49	```
50	
51	With `mamba`, one can create the virtual environment with:
52	
53	```bash
54	mamba create -n pgkyl
55	```
56	
57	then activate with:
58	
59	```bash
60	mamba activate pgkyl
61	```
62	
63	and deactivate with:
64	
65	```bash
66	mamba deactivate
67	```
68	
69	Note that with `mamba`, one can also use the provided `environment.yml` file,
70	which also includes dependency specifications:
71	
72	```bash
73	mamba env create -f environment.yml
74	```
75	
76	### Installing Postgkyl
77	
78	The Postgkyl itself is installed with `pip`.[^1] Developers and uses who want to
79	have the most up-to-date version should install Postgkyl from the source code:
80	
81	```bash
82	git clone https://github.com/ammarhakim/postgkyl.git
83	cd postgkyl
84	pip install -e .[test]
85	```
86	
87	Alternatively, Postgkyl can be installed directly from [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/postgkyl/):
88	
89	```bash
90	pip install -e postgkyl[test]
91	```
92	
93	#### The Gkeyll bridge (native `.gkyl` reading, `interpolate`, weak algebra)
94	
95	Postgkyl talks to Gkeyll through a small compiled bridge (`gpython`), not a path you configure. **This is
96	built automatically** as part of `pip install`/`pip install -e .`. `setup.py` runs
97	`scripts/build_gkeyll.sh`, which:
98	
99	1. clones [Gkeyll](https://github.com/ammarhakim/gkeyll) into `./gkeyll/`
100	   (a sparse, blobless, depth-1 clone of just the `core/` app — a few tens
101	   of MB, not a submodule),
102	2. `./configure`s and `make core`s it into `gkeyll/build/core/libg0core.so`
103	   with no external dependencies (`--use-lapack-lite=yes`, so no
104	   MPI/CUDA/SuperLU/Lua/system LAPACK are required), then
105	3. compiles postgkyl's `_gpython` CPython extension
106	   (`src/postgkyl/gpython/csrc/_gpythonmodule.c`) against it.
107	
108	This step needs **network access** (to clone Gkeyll) and **a C compiler**.
109	It defaults to `cc`; if your system doesn't have `cc`, set `CC=gcc` (or any compiler you have) before
110	installing:
111	```bash
112	CC=gcc pip install -e .[test]
113	```
114	
115	The extension targets NumPy's `>=2.2` ABI explicitly (matching the `numpy>=2.2.6`
116	floor above), so it stays loadable even though `pip` may build it against a
117	different NumPy release than the one that ends up installed (its isolated
118	build environment resolves `numpy` independently). If you ever see a `numpy.dtype
119	size changed` error on import, that means the NumPy actually installed is
120	below this floor; reinstalling with `pip install -e .[test] --no-build-isolation`
121	forces the build to reuse your already-installed NumPy and sidesteps that
122	resolution entirely.
123	
124	If this step fails or is skipped, Postgkyl still imports and works — reading
125	files falls back to a pure-Python reader, and anything that needs the
126	compiled bridge (`.interpolate()`, weak `* /` on modal data, native `.gkyl`
127	reading, `.integrate()`, …) raises a `RuntimeError` naming the missing piece
128	instead of the pipeline silently doing the wrong thing. Check whether the
129	bridge is active with:
130	```bash
131	python -c "from postgkyl import gpython; print(gpython.available())"
132	```
133	
134	To rebuild by hand (e.g. after pulling a Postgkyl or Gkeyll update, or after
135	fixing a compiler issue), re-run either script from the repo root — both are
136	safe to re-run:
137	```bash
138	scripts/build_gkeyll.sh   # full: re-clone/build libg0core.so, then the extension
139	scripts/build_gpython.sh  # just the extension, if libg0core.so is already built
140	```
141	
142	If `gpython.available()` is `False`, the printed error explains which of the
143	two prerequisites (compiler, or the clone) is missing, or whether the built
144	extension is stale relative to the shim header — the fix in that last case
145	is always `scripts/build_gpython.sh`.
146	
147	## Testing
148	
149	Postgkyl utilizes [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/) for testing. The tests can
150	be called manually from the root Postgkyl directory simply by using:
151	
152	```bash
153	pytest [-v]
154	```
155	
156	## Authors
157	
158	The full list of authors can be found [here](AUTHORS.md).
159	
160	## License
161	
162	Postgkyl is distributed under the MIT License.

165	    Postgkyl was used previously through `PYTHONPATH`, we strongly recommend
166	    removing the path to the Postgkyl repository from the variable.

Found it — two separate issues in that transcript:

**1. The `setup.py not found` error** happened before you `checkout refactor-diagnostics`. That's just because you were on `main`'s worktree state before switching branches — a non-issue, already resolved by your `git checkout` + `pull`.

**2. The real blocker:** `pip install -e .` failed with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'setuptools.command.editable_wheel'`. Your fresh venv came with **pip 9.0.3** (from 2018) and whatever ancient `setuptools` ships alongside it. `editable_wheel` is a PEP 660 feature that only exists in `setuptools >= 64` — this repo's `setup.py:7` imports it directly, so an old setuptools can't even parse the file.

Fix: upgrade pip/setuptools/wheel inside the venv *before* installing postgkyl:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
pip install -e .[test]
```

Given `stellar-vis2` sounds like an HPC cluster node, the venv's bootstrap pip is likely tied to whatever system Python module was loaded — worth confirming `python3 --version` is reasonably recent (3.10+) too, since a very old system Python can also mean an old bundled pip that resists upgrading cleanly.

One more thing from the README worth flagging in advance: the install step needs network access and a C compiler (it clones and builds Gkeyll's core). If `cc` isn't on that machine's PATH, you'll need `CC=gcc pip install -e .[test]` (or whatever compiler module the cluster provides).


The root cause: on this cluster, `module load anaconda3/2024.10` has a side effect of implicitly running `conda activate base` — that's what gave you Python 3.12.7 last time. `deactivate` un-does that conda activation, but Lmod treats `anaconda3` as already loaded, so the second `module load anaconda3/2024.10` was a no-op — it didn't redo the implicit `conda activate base`. So when you ran `python3 -m venv .venv`, `python3` had already fallen back to the system's ancient 3.6.8, and that old interpreter got baked into the new venv.

Fix: don't rely on the module's side effect — activate conda explicitly, verify the version, build the venv from it, then get conda's `base` out of the way *before* activating the venv (so it can't get shadowed again):

```bash
module purge
module load anaconda3/2024.10
conda activate base
python3 --version              # must show 3.12.x here, before touching .venv

rm -rf .venv
python3 -m venv .venv
conda deactivate                # drop base now, so it can't shadow .venv/bin afterward
source .venv/bin/activate

which python3                   # should be .venv/bin/python3
python3 --version               # should be 3.12.x
which pip

pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
pip install -e .[test]
```

The key ordering change from before: `conda deactivate` happens *after* the venv is built from the right interpreter but *before* `source .venv/bin/activate`, so there's no conda `base` left on `PATH` to race with the venv's own `bin/`.

Full from-scratch setup using `pyenv` to get a modern, standalone Python — no Anaconda module involved anywhere, so there's no `conda activate`/`deactivate` PATH-shadowing risk at all.

```bash
# 1. Get the code
git clone https://github.com/gkeyllorg/postgkyl.git
cd postgkyl
git checkout refactor-diagnostics
git pull

# 2. Install pyenv (pure user-space, no sudo required)
git clone https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv.git ~/.pyenv

# Add to your shell rc (~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc) so it's available in future sessions:
echo 'export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'command -v pyenv >/dev/null || export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'eval "$(pyenv init -)"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

# 3. Build a modern Python (this compiles CPython from source — needs a C
#    compiler; if the cluster's default `cc` is missing, load one first,
#    e.g. `module load gcc` if such a module exists here)
pyenv install 3.12.7
pyenv local 3.12.7          # pins this directory to 3.12.7 via .python-version
python3 --version           # confirm: 3.12.7, and check `which python3` -> ~/.pyenv/...

# 4. Build the venv from that interpreter
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

which python3                # sanity check: must point into .venv/bin
python3 --version            # must still be 3.12.7

# 5. Upgrade packaging tools, then install postgkyl + test deps
#    (this also builds the Gkeyll bridge: needs network access + a C compiler)
pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
pip install -e .[test]
# If `cc` isn't found:
# CC=gcc pip install -e .[test]

# 6. Verify
python3 -c "from postgkyl import gpython; print(gpython.available())"
pgkyl --version
pytest
```

Two things to watch for during `pyenv install`, since this cluster likely has no `sudo`:
- If the build log warns that the `_ssl` module failed to build, `pip` won't be able to fetch packages from PyPI at all — that means the system is missing OpenSSL dev headers. Check `module avail openssl` (or similar) and `module load` it before running `pyenv install` again.
- Other optional warnings (`_bz2`, `_lzma`, `_tkinter`, etc.) are safe to ignore — postgkyl doesn't need them.

For future sessions, just `cd postgkyl && source .venv/bin/activate` — `pyenv`'s shell hook (from step 2) plus the `.python-version` file will keep `python3` resolving correctly even before you activate the venv.

You skipped the pyenv steps and built the venv straight from the system's `python3.6.8` — that's why it's still old. Here's how to fix it in place:

```bash
# 1. Tear down the bad venv
deactivate
rm -rf .venv

# 2. Install pyenv if you haven't already (skip if ~/.pyenv already exists)
git clone https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv.git ~/.pyenv
export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"
eval "$(pyenv init -)"

# 3. Build a modern Python (needs a C compiler; `module load gcc` first if `cc` isn't on PATH)
pyenv install 3.12.7

# 4. Create the venv using that interpreter's binary DIRECTLY —
#    bypasses any PATH/shim ordering questions entirely
~/.pyenv/versions/3.12.7/bin/python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

which python3       # must be .venv/bin/python3
python3 --version   # must be 3.12.7

# 5. Install
pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
pip install -e .[test]
```

The key fix is step 4: instead of running bare `python3 -m venv .venv` (which just uses whatever `python3` happens to be first on `PATH` — the ancient system one, in your last run), you invoke pyenv's installed interpreter by its full path. That guarantees the venv is built from 3.12.7 regardless of how `PATH`/shims are set up in the current shell.

Provide a clean set of installation instructions to install postgkyl inside a conda environment

Clean install using a dedicated `conda` environment instead of a `venv` — this sidesteps the `venv`/`conda activate` PATH-shadowing issues entirely, since there's no venv layered on top:

```bash
# 1. Get the code
git clone https://github.com/gkeyllorg/postgkyl.git
cd postgkyl
git checkout refactor-diagnostics
git pull

# 2. Load conda and create a dedicated environment for postgkyl
module purge
module load anaconda3/2024.10
conda create -n pgkyl python=3.12 -y
conda activate pgkyl

which python3                  # sanity check: must point into the pgkyl env
python3 --version              # should be 3.12.x
which pip

# 3. Install postgkyl + test deps into this environment
#    (this also builds the Gkeyll bridge: needs network access + a C compiler)
pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
pip install -e .[test]
# If `cc` isn't found on this system:
# CC=gcc pip install -e .[test]

# 4. Verify
python3 -c "from postgkyl import gpython; print(gpython.available())"
pgkyl --version
pytest
```

For future sessions, just:
```bash
module purge
module load anaconda3/2024.10
conda activate pgkyl
```
from anywhere — no need to `cd` into the repo first or re-source anything, since the environment is registered with conda by name rather than living as a path-relative `.venv/` folder.

Alternative: since `environment.yml` already lists postgkyl's dependencies, you can create and populate the environment in one step instead of steps 2–3:
```bash
module purge && module load anaconda3/2024.10
conda env create -f environment.yml -n pgkyl
conda activate pgkyl
pip install -e . --no-deps   # editable-install postgkyl itself into the env just built
```
`--no-deps` here avoids pip re-resolving/reinstalling everything `environment.yml` already set up via conda.
